en: The Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty.
The Buddha is the most honored among all sages; his supernormal powers and responses are sovereign and autonomous.
Manifesting bodies according to the various types of beings, their voices are likewise so;
those who see or hear them obtain peace and security—let none fail to have a mind of faith and devotion.
Therefore, I take refuge [in you], and pray that I may become like the World-Honored One everywhere.
The profound Bodhisattva precepts possess inconceivable merit;
Those who receive them obtain peace and security, And virtue and wisdom arise day and night.
The Buddhas always protect and mind them, Until the myriad practices gradually reach full completion.
With the intention of the six perfections and the four immeasurables, universally delivering all who are blind;
never violating the conduct of hands and feet at the outset, moderating speech and acting in accordance with what one does;
always delighting in a concentrated mind—this is called a true bhikṣu.
"Sincere and upright, free from flattery and crookedness, always associating with the noble and holy,
loving the multitude as if nourishing oneself— this is called a true Bodhisattva.
O Venerable Ones!"
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I now wish to expound the precepts of merit that accomplish the benefit of all sentient beings, as realized by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
For one who abides thus in the bodhisattva precepts, there are four *pārājika* dharmas. What are these four?
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and honor, praises himself and disparages others, this is called a bodhisattva *pārājika*.

If a bodhisattva possesses abundant wealth, yet when a person in poverty and suffering comes to beg from him, the bodhisattva is stingy and greedy, lacking any heart of compassion, and does not bestow even a single coin; or if there is one who seeks the Dharma, he does not even explain a single verse for them—this is called a bodhisattva’s *pārājika*.

If a bodhisattva, out of anger, reviles and insults another with harsh words, and further strikes them with his hands or with sticks and stones, yet his mind still does not cease; and even when the other person seeks reconciliation with kind words and offers an apology, the bodhisattva remains filled with rage and resentment that he cannot resolve—this is called a bodhisattva’s *pārājika*.

If a bodhisattva slanders the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas themselves, or sees others slandering it and approves of their words, or having personally lost faith, instead assists others in their speech—whether this arises from one's own understanding or is received from another—this is called a bodhisattva pārājika offense.
Thus, regarding these four *pārājika* offenses of a bodhisattva, a bodhisattva should not commit even one of them, much less all of them!
If one commits them, they are no longer called a bodhisattva.
One who manifests in bodily form yet cannot adorn bodhi, nor can bring the mind to tranquility, is a semblance Bodhisattva, not a true Bodhisattva.
There are three grades of such transgressions:
inferior, middling, and superior.
If one commits an offense with a weak or middling mind, it is not termed a "loss.
If one commits an offense with a superior mind, it is termed a "loss.
What is meant by "superior"?
If one commits any of the four aforementioned offenses repeatedly with pleasure, lacking a sense of shame or remorse and failing to reproach oneself, this is called a "grave offense.
Although a bodhisattva may commit these four grave offenses, they do not immediately and permanently lose [their status].
For example, if a bhikṣu commits the four [parājika offenses], he is immediately and permanently cast out.
It is not so for a bodhisattva. Why is this?
If a bhikṣu commits an offense, there is no way for him to receive the precepts again;
although a bodhisattva may commit an offense, he can still receive them anew, and for this reason they are not the same.
Briefly, there are two matters by which one loses the bodhisattva precepts: first, abandoning the vow for enlightenment; second, the arising of a superior evil mind.
Except for these two matters, if one maintains this body and precepts, they will never be lost.

From this point forward, in every place of rebirth, one will always possess these precepts. Even if one does not consciously recollect them, should one encounter virtuous friends and receive them again, this is not called "newly obtaining" them.

Regarding such Bodhisattva precepts, one should recognize the characteristics of the gravity of transgressions and non-transgressions, as well as their distinctions as inferior, middling, or superior.

One who abides in these Bodhisattva precepts should daily make offerings to the Buddhas, whether in person, as stupas, or as images; next, they should make offerings to the Dharma, those who practice the Dharma, and the Mahāyāna scriptures of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; and they should make offerings to the Saṃgha and to all Bodhisattvas dwelling on the great earth throughout the ten directions.

Throughout the day and night, make offerings to the Triple Gem according to your capacity; even if it is but a single thought-moment, a single prostration, or the recitation of a single four-line verse, offer them with faith and do not allow such practice to cease.
If one fails to show respect due to arrogance or a state of mental depression, one commits a grave secondary offense (*gurutara-āpatti*).
If it was through forgetfulness or error, one commits a light secondary offense (*laghu-āpatti*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill or insane; if one possesses a pure mind and has attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, or has attained the indestructible pure mind like a *srotāpanna*, and is constantly able to make offerings to the Triple Gem without interruption—this is called having no offense.
If a bodhisattva does not know contentment, being greedily attached to gain and offerings and failing to restrain the mind, they commit a grave defiled offense.
There is no offense if, although they are greedy for gain and offerings, they constantly give rise to a sense of regret, thinking:
"I shall apply myself with diligence to sever this intention."
"If, despite extreme self-restraint, a greedy mind still arises, or if one takes a small benefit to assist in severing great greed, this is called no offense.

"If a Bodhisattva, upon seeing a senior elder, a venerable person, an aged one, or one of equal virtue, teacher, or fellow student, gives rise to a mind of arrogance or a mind of anger and malice, failing to rise to greet them, pay homage, or yield his seat; or if, when there is speech or conversation, he does not listen, or if asked something, he does not answer according to reality, he commits a grave defiled offense."

If one commits this offense with a mind free from pride, anger, or delusion, but solely through indolence, a neutral state of mind, or a distracted mind, it constitutes a light secondary offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill, if one is insane, if one is asleep at the time, if one is listening to or preaching the Dharma, if one is previously engaged in conversation with another, if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness, or if there are monastic restrictions or the need to protect the feelings of many people. These are called cases where there is no offense.

"If a bodhisattva, when invited by a donor to receive whatever is required—whether at their own home or within a monastery—does not go to accept it due to arrogance, anger, or contempt, they commit a grave defiled offense."
If one fails to go due to laziness, one commits a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases:

if one is ill; if one is insane; if the place is distant; if the path is dangerous and difficult; if it is for the purpose of subduing others, extinguishing evil, or increasing goodness; if one has lost the invitation; if it is for the purpose of cultivating virtue; if it is to hear what has not been heard before; if one knows that the host intends to cause harassment; or if there are restrictions by the Sangha intended to protect the sentiments of many people. These are called non-offenses.

"A Bodhisattva, when obtaining from others various necessary items such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and assorted precious gems, as well as hidden treasures in the earth that have no owner, should take them all, mindful that they shall be further bestowed upon others."
If one does not accept [the gift] due to an evil mind of anger, one commits a grave defiled offense.
If one forms this thought: "I will not give to others."
If one creates such conditions out of a lazy mind, one commits a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is deranged; if it is for the purpose of subduing [the mind] to eliminate evil and increase goodness; if one knows that upon receiving [the gift], attachment will inevitably arise; if one knows that the donor will feel regret after giving; if one knows that the donor has become insane because of the act of giving; if one fears that the donor will fall into poverty and suffering after giving; if one knows that the object of the gift belongs to the Triple Gem; if one knows that the object of the gift was obtained through robbery or theft; if one knows that upon receiving it, one will experience much suffering—namely, royal persecution, banditry, death, imprisonment, the spread of ill repute, or being banished from the realm. These are called cases of no offense.
“If a bodhisattva, when someone comes to seek the Dharma, does not teach it because of a mind of anger, malice, or envy toward that person, they commit a grave secondary offense (gurutara-pāyattika).
If they do not teach it out of a mind of laziness, they commit a minor secondary offense.”

There is no offense in the following cases: if a non-Buddhist seeks the Dharma out of fear that they might subsequently disparage it; if one is ill or insane; if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; if one knows that the other person does not understand its meaning; if the other person lacks respect or acts contrary to the Dharma; if the other person has dull faculties and would not understand the profound Dharma, fearing they might give rise to wrong views; if one knows that upon hearing it, they would lose their original mind and destroy the True Dharma; or if one knows that upon hearing it, they would inevitably proclaim the matter to those who are not suitable vessels. These are called cases where there is no offense.

"If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are evil, who violate the precepts and prohibitions, and commit various sinful deeds, and yet the bodhisattva knows they can be transformed into goodness—if, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, he abandons them and fails to instruct them, he commits a grave defiling offense."
Why is this? A bodhisattva does not give rise to compassion toward those who maintain the precepts purely in body, speech, and mind.
Rather, when they see an evil person who violates the precepts, breaks the prohibitions, and commits various misdeeds, they give rise to extreme compassion; for this reason, there is transgression.

There is no offense if one is insane; or if it is for the purpose of subduing [the person] to extinguish evil and increase goodness; or if there is a restriction by the Saṃgha to protect the intentions of many people—these are called non-offenses.

“Bodhisattva, regarding the prātimokṣa and the formulated vinaya as established by the Buddha—intended to cause those without faith to have faith and to increase the faith of those who already have it—the śrāvaka precepts and the bodhisattva precepts are no different from one another.”

Why is this? Because even śrāvakas act according to their own constant practice, yet they still desire to study so as to cause those who do not believe to believe and those who already believe to increase in faith.
How much more so for the training cultivated by a bodhisattva, which is always for the sake of sentient beings—how could such a person not be able to do this!
For this reason, it is called "identical" and thus there is no offense.
As the Buddha has prescribed, those who are śrāvakas should have few desires and engage in few causal activities;
the bodhisattva is not like this.
Why is this? To seek one's own benefit in accordance with desire, without acting for the sake of others, is the preference of a śrāvaka.
If a bodhisattva were thus, they would not be called a bodhisattva.
For the sake of others, one may accept as many as a hundred thousand robes, having sought them with all one's effort from non-relatives, whether Brahmins or householders.
As it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls.

For the sake of others, as well as requesting thread, instructing weavers to weave, keeping *kauśeya* silk garments, and accepting gold and silver—even up to hundreds of thousands—such matters differ from those of the śrāvakas.

If a bodhisattva, having originally taken up the task for the sake of sentient beings, gives rise to a mind of anger or malice and, due to minor actions or slight causes and conditions, abandons sentient beings to dwell alone in solitude, he commits a grave defiled offense.
If one harbors a lazy mind and dwells in their place with few desires and few affairs, they commit a minor offense.
"A Bodhisattva has five unlawful practices:
first, flattery; second, vanity; third, ostentation; fourth, seeking profit through profit; and fifth, wrong livelihood."
If one possesses these five conditions yet feels no shame and neither restrains nor ceases [the offense], one commits a grave defiled offense (*gurutara-āpatti*).
There is no offense if, perceiving it as contrary to the Dharma, one constantly desires to restrain it; this is called "no offense."

If a bodhisattva, out of frivolity or distraction, speaks aloud and in a loud voice, acting in a manner contrary to dignified decorum so as to cause others to laugh and be held in contempt by the assembly, they commit a grave defiling offense.
If one commits this through the negligence of past habituation, one incurs a minor offense (light defilement).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one realizes it is contrary to the Dharma and constantly intends to restrain it; if it is for the sake of subduing an outsider who is full of anger; if it is to relieve the suffering and distress of someone; if it is for the sake of gathering others together through playful jesting; or if it is to reconcile two people who are quarreling. These are called non-offenses.
“A bodhisattva sees thus and speaks thus:
‘A bodhisattva should not delight in nirvāṇa; he should turn away from nirvāṇa. He should not fear the afflictions (kleśa), nor should he extinguish the afflictions.’”
"Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas undergo birth and death through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
One who speaks such words commits a grave defiling offense.
Why is this? If one were to compare a bodhisattva’s delight in nirvāṇa and dread of afflictions to those of a śrāvaka, it would be a thousand-million-fold difference beyond all analogy. Why is this?
The śrāvaka acts for his own sake alone, whereas the bodhisattva always acts for the sake of all sentient beings.
Although the bodhisattva dwells amidst outflows (sāsrava), he attains mastery over the extinction of afflictions; thus, he surpasses the arhat who dwells in the state of outflowlessness (anāsrava).
If a bodhisattva gives rise to physical or verbal karma, they should personally guard against it so as not to cause others to fall into the sin of indolence.
If one intentionally fails to guard oneself and causes others to incur the sin of indolence, one commits a grave defiled offense.
If one fails to mindfully protect oneself and, through negligent conduct, causes others to commit offenses, one commits a minor secondary offense (light impurity).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it concerns non-Buddhists; if one acts in accordance with the Dharma while following those who have left the household life; or if one encounters persons of great anger and malice. These are called cases of no offense.
"If a Bodhisattva, seeing that sentient beings before them would benefit only after being subjected to the pain of a staff, fails to treat them out of self-protection, they commit a minor offense.
There is no offense if the benefit would be slight while the suffering would be great; this is called non-offense."

“If a bodhisattva responds to verbal abuse with verbal abuse, responds to anger with anger, responds to physical assault with physical assault, or drags and pulls another, they commit a grave defiled offense.

“If a bodhisattva engages in a quarrel with another or harbors mutual resentment, and with a mind of malice, anger, or pride fails to repent according to the Dharma, they commit a grave defiled offense.”
If one is lazy and negligent, and does not seek repentance even once, one commits a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is for the purpose of subduing [the person] to extinguish evil and increase goodness; if that outsider intends to perform what is contrary to the Dharma; if that person delights in strife and resentment would only increase further; if one knows that the person will ultimately not accept repentance; or if repenting toward them would cause them to give rise to grave arrogance. These are called non-offenses.

"If a bodhisattva harbors resentment toward another, and that other person seeks reconciliation in accordance with the Dharma, yet the bodhisattva, out of malice, refuses to accept it in order to cause them distress, he commits a grave defiled offense."
If one harbors no anger yet refuses to accept another's apology, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of subduing [the offender], extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; or if the other person is wicked and unrighteous—these are called non-offenses.
"If a bodhisattva harbors anger toward another recipient and does not cease the object of that anger, they commit a grave defiled offense.
There is no offense if they constantly restrain it, yet the angry mind still arises; this is called no offense."
"If a bodhisattva accepts and maintains a retinue of disciples solely for the purpose of providing them with service, food, and clothing, this is called an offense.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a lazy mind, delights in eating at improper times, or becomes greedily attached to sleep—whether reclining or lying down—he commits a grave defiled offense."

There is no offense if one is ill, or insane, or lacks skillful means; or if one is exhausted from traveling on a road; or if it is something one habitually restrains oneself from. These are called non-offenses.
"If a Bodhisattva, with a mind of attachment, speaks of worldly pleasures, they commit a grave defiling offense."
If one speaks erroneously out of forgetfulness, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

There is no offense if someone asks a question and one speaks briefly with a correct mind; or if one discusses unusual accounts; or if one discusses matters concerning the Dharma. These are called non-offenses.

"If a bodhisattva desires to practice dhyāna and knows that another possesses the Dharma, yet, due to a mind of anger or pride, is unable to humble himself and seek to receive the Dharma from that person, he commits a grave defiled offense."
If one commits the offense of minor defilement due to a lazy mind that does not seek to receive [the teachings], it is an offense.

There is no offense if one is ill, lacks skillful means, knows that the person is not compliant with the Dharma teachings, or if one possesses skillful means and extensive learning to restrain one's own mind. This is called no offense.
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to desire for the realm of desire and does not contemplate its antidote so that it is swiftly eliminated, they commit a grave defiled offense.
There is no offense if, despite being constantly diligent in wishing to extinguish desire, the mind of desire still arises; this is called 'no offense.'"
As it is with desire, so it is with the other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
If a bodhisattva craves the flavor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and becomes attached to its merits, they commit a grave defiled offense (*sāvadya-guruka-pāpa*).
There is no offense if they constantly intend to abandon attachment, yet an attached mind still arises; this is called "no offense."
“A bodhisattva sees thus and speaks thus:
‘A bodhisattva should not listen to, receive, recite, or study the scriptural collection of the śrāvakas.
What purpose would there be for a person who is a bodhisattva to study this?’”
One who speaks such words commits a grave offense of defilement.
Why is this? A bodhisattva should study even the scriptures of non-Buddhists, let alone the words of the Buddha!
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of subduing śrāvakas so that they may enter the Mahāyāna; this is called "no offense.

However, if one completely neglects the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas and greedily studies, reads, and recites only the sūtras of the śrāvakas, one commits a minor secondary offense (light defilement).
"If a bodhisattva does not diligently study the scriptural treasury of the Buddha, but instead diligently studies the secular texts of non-Buddhists, they commit a grave offense of defilement.

There is no offense if: their faculties are extremely sharp such that they can retain [the teachings] upon hearing them once; or if they take up [non-Buddhist texts] as being identical to the Buddha’s words in order to assist in conversion; or if they use those excellent expressions to help clarify the Buddha-dharma, without wavering from the meaning and intent of the Buddha-dharma and the Buddha’s scriptures. This is called having no offense."
"A Bodhisattva who wishes to study the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths should study them as described above.
If, however, they experience pleasure therein and give rise to a mind of attachment—failing to regard it like taking bitter medicine—they commit a grave offense of defilement."

“Bodhisattva, if one hears the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas—its profound secrets, its supreme ultimate reality, and its inconceivable matters—which belong solely to the domain of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—and yet conceives a mind of slander toward this meaning, saying:
‘This meaning is useless; it was not spoken by the Buddha; it cannot benefit or bring aid to all sentient beings.’”
One who slanders in this manner commits a grave offense of defilement.
There is no offense in cases where one is contemplating the meaning of the Dharma or speaking as a skillful means; these are called non-offenses.
“Bodhisattvas, when hearing profound meanings, if they do not give rise to faith, they should, with a mind free from guile and for the sake of generating faith, reflect thus:
‘I ought not to be like this.’”
"I am like one who is blind and lacks the eye of wisdom.
How could I slander what has been spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth?
In this way, the bodhisattva reproaches himself for his delusion, thinking, "This is the domain of the Buddhas; it is not within my reach. To be able to act in such a manner is correct practice.
If one does not harbor malice and does not give rise to slander, this is called non-offense.
"If a bodhisattva, for the sake of food and drink, with a mind of anger and ill-will, praises themselves and disparages others, they commit a grave defiled offense."

There is no offense if it is for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists, or for subduing pride to increase the Buddha-dharma, or for causing those who lack faith to have faith and increasing the faith of those who already possess it; this is called "no offense."

“If a bodhisattva, out of anger, envy, or pride, does not go to listen when there is a place where the Dharma is being taught, or where the Vinaya is being recited, or at a great assembly of the Dharma, they commit a grave defiled offense.”
If one fails to go and listen due to a lazy mind, one commits a minor offense (light impurity). There is no offense in the following cases:

if one does not hear it oneself and there is no one to summon one; if one is ill or lacks the skillful means; if one knows that the teaching being given does not accord with the principles of meaning; if one knows that the speaker will pose difficulties for oneself; if one knows that what is being said has already been heard elsewhere; if one has attained *dhāraṇī* and is already widely learned; or if one is diligently cultivating roots of goodness. These are called non-offenses.

“Bodhisattva, suppose someone comes to request your assistance, saying, ‘I have certain matters to attend to and you should manage them for me,’ namely: going and returning together, assisting in various affairs, managing and completing tasks, guarding property, mediating disputes, preparing food and drink, and cultivating meritorious deeds.

If one fails to perform one or two such tasks, one commits a grave offense of defilement (*gurutara-āpatti*). If one fails to perform them due to laziness, one commits a minor offense of defilement (*laghu-āpatti*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one lacks skillful means; if one has one's own business; if the other person is capable of managing it; if one has not been requested to do so; if it is a useless task; if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; if there is no one else to request; if it is to repay another for their labor by diligently cultivating roots of goodness; if one is dull-witted and fears losing the sequence of one’s duties; or if there is a monastic restriction to protect the sentiments of the many. These are called non-offenses.
"If a bodhisattva, upon seeing a sick sentient being, fails to provide care and sustenance due to an evil mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiling offense.
If they fail to provide care and sustenance due to laziness, they commit a minor defiling offense."

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is personally ill; if one lacks skillful means; if one has requested another to attend to the patient; if the patient already has their own relatives; if one knows the patient is capable of providing for themselves; if the illness is chronic; if the person is still able to rise and sit up; if one wishes to diligently cultivate superior roots of goodness; if one is extremely dull-witted and fears losing their place in the sequence; or if the loss of nursing care is equivalent to the loss of the illness itself. The same applies to cases of poverty and suffering. These are called non-offenses.
"If a Bodhisattva perceives that there is a beneficial purpose for sentient beings before them, yet fails to initiate action because they lack the skillful means,
and does not provide instruction due to an evil mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiled offense."
If one fails to instruct due to laziness, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one lacks the skillful means; if one has commissioned another to instruct; if the person already possesses their own spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); if it is for the purpose of subduing them to eliminate evil and increase goodness; or if, when shown skillful means, they become even more angry and perverse, lacking respect and affection while stubbornly insisting on their own way—these are called non-offenses.
“A Bodhisattva, when sentient beings provide them with what they require, should be mindful of their kindness.
If, with an evil mind or a mind of anger, one fails to be mindful of or repay that kindness, one commits a grave defiled offense.”
If one fails to repay out of laziness, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one lacks personal capability; if one lacks skillful means; if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; or if one intends to repay but the donor does not accept it. These are called non-offenses.
"If a bodhisattva, seeing that a relative has died or that someone has suffered various anxieties and sufferings due to the loss of wealth,
fails to go and offer consolation out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiled offense."
There is no offense in cases as previously explained regarding the bodhisattva who accepts requests.
"If a bodhisattva, when someone comes to him seeking food or drink, does not give what is required, he commits a grave defiling offense."

There is no offense if one has no property of one's own, or if one requests impure items, or if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness, or if it is prohibited by the king, or if it is to protect the limits of the Sangha; these are called non-offenses.
“A Bodhisattva should instruct and admonish their disciples according to the occasion.
If a disciple is in need, the Bodhisattva should encourage a person of firm faith to provide for them.
If, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, one fails to instruct or provide for them, one commits a grave defiled offense.”
If, out of a lazy mind, one fails to instruct [the disciple] on how to provide offerings, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is for the purpose of subduing [the disciple], extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; if it is to protect the boundaries of the Sangha; if one is ill; if one lacks skillful means; if one has entrusted another person with the instruction; if the disciple’s own merit is sufficient to procure offerings; or if the disciple was originally a non-Buddhist and lacks a wholesome, virtuous mind. These are called cases of no offense.
"If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of anger or an evil mind, fails to protect the intentions of others, they commit a grave defiled offense.
If they fail to protect the intentions of others due to laziness or negligence, they commit a minor defiled offense."

There is no offense if it concerns an unlawful matter, if one is ill, if there is a restriction by the Sangha for the sake of protecting the minds of many people, if it concerns a non-Buddhist, or if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; these are called non-offenses.
"If a Bodhisattva, upon seeing the virtuous conduct of others, fails to praise it and instead conceals their goodness out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiled offense.
If they fail to praise the goodness of others due to laziness or negligence, they commit a minor defiled offense."

There is no offense if one knows that the person does not delight in praise; or if they are ill; or if one lacks skillful means; or if it is for the purpose of subduing them to eliminate evil and increase goodness; or if it is to protect the boundaries of the Sangha; or if one knows that hearing praise would only give rise to further arrogance; or if the person lacks genuine virtue; or if the words appear to be good but in reality lack virtuous meaning; or if they are a non-Buddhist; or if the time for praise has not yet arrived—these are called cases of no offense.
"A Bodhisattva, acting as a leader among many people, sees that his retinue is engaging in unrighteous conduct and ought to be reprimanded or expelled.
If, out of a mind of anger or malice, he neglects to reprimand or discipline them, he commits a grave defiling offense."
If one is lazy or negligent and fails to instruct or admonish [the offender], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

There is no offense if: one knows that the person is of an evil nature, prone to anger, and will not accept instruction or admonition; if one intends to instruct or admonish them at a later time; if one fears it would cause a schism in the Sangha; or if one knows that the person is upright by nature, has few latent tendencies, possesses a sense of shame, and takes pleasure in repenting for frequent transgressions. These are called cases of no offense.

"A Bodhisattva possesses supernatural powers and transformations; they should manifest them for sentient beings according to the occasion, or employ skillful means to inspire awe so that faith may arise.
If, out of fear of offerings given in faith, one fails to manifest such transformations, one commits a minor offense."

There is no offense in the following cases: if a person is deeply attached to unwholesome dharmas and wrong views; if they are a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); if they revile the noble ones (ārya); if they are possessed by wrong views; or if they are insane or afflicted by illness. These are called non-offenses.

“Bodhisattvas, having fully accomplished the aggregate of precepts, possess immeasurable and wondrous fruits; by the power of the causal conditions of this aggregate of precepts, they fulfill the śīla-pāramitā.”
Although the recipient has not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they have acquired five kinds of meritorious qualities:
first, they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
second, they receive constant, pure bliss.
Third, one will have no regrets at the time of death;
fourth, upon casting off the body, one will attain rebirth in the worlds of the Buddhas;
fifth, one will adorn *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts does not act for their own sake, but solely for the benefit of others and for the adornment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This Bodhisattva precept is that which has been accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even so it is for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.

The Bodhisattva’s vast compassion and universal grace reach all sentient beings of the six realms and those in the three miserable paths and eight difficulties; throughout the ten directions, there are none who do not receive benefit from his suffering-relieving aid.
His merit is incalculable, and his blessings and wisdom are like space.
Having briefly concluded this summary of the essential points, rejoice and pay homage as you practice accordingly.
Universally giving rise to the bodhicitta, The life-force of merit and wisdom is perfected;
Compassion grows long within sons and daughters, And joy and equanimity arise in succession.
All shall attain the path of Buddhahood, Forever reaching the end with nothing remaining.
“The ten directions share in his vow; he is the Sublime One, majestic and infinite.

“If one wishes to become a bodhisattva upāsaka who observes the five precepts and dignified conduct, yet has no teacher from whom to receive them, then at that time, if there is no teacher, the recipient should take the vow before an image of the Buddha by means of a personal oath.”

A Bodhisattva Upāsaka should perform the ritual of prostration in this manner: baring the right shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms, he should speak as follows:

"I, [Name], address the Buddhas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas dwelling upon the Great Earth. Now, in the presence of all Buddhas, I wish to receive all the precepts: I shall train in all Bodhisattva precepts, the ritual decorum of the five precepts of an Upāsaka, the Bodhisattva precepts that encompass all wholesome dharmas, and the precepts for the benefit of sentient beings."

This precept has been studied by all bodhisattvas of the past, shall be studied by all bodhisattvas of the future, and is being studied now by all bodhisattvas of the present; I, too, study it in this same way.
The second and third [recitations] were likewise spoken in full.
The remaining matters should be explained in detail as previously stated:
"A lay follower who has renounced desire fully observes the five precepts and remains far removed from the four bodily evils."
First is killing, second is stealing, third is sexual misconduct, and fourth is drinking alcohol.
One should distance oneself from the five evils of speech:
first, lying; second, harsh speech; third, divisive speech; fourth, idle speech; and fifth, frivolous speech.
One should distance oneself from the five forms of wrong livelihood:
first, selling meat; second, selling intoxicants; third, selling poisons; fourth, selling living beings; and fifth, selling weapons.
One should distance oneself from five types of adornments:
first, incense; second, flowers; third, necklaces and ornaments; fourth, the anointing of the body with fragrant oils; and fifth, clothing perfumed with incense.
There are five matters from which one should distance oneself regarding negligence:
first, singing; second, dancing; third, performing music; fourth, decorating musical instruments; and fifth, going to watch or listen to them.
These five precepts may be undertaken according to one's capacity. If one is able to maintain all five throughout one's entire life, that is best;
if not, one may observe them for as long as possible—whether for months, years, days, or nights—even if only for a brief moment, it is still permissible to hold them temporarily.
Not only as in the case of maintaining mindfulness;
when the Buddha was on the verge of entering *parinirvāṇa*, he instructed the four great *śrāvakas* and the six *arhats*:

"After my passing, within this True Dharma, if those in the two monastic communities maintain the prohibitive precepts purely, and those in the two lay communities, according to their respective means, maintain the higher precepts with a focused mind, they should construct dwellings, bedding, clothing, food, drink, and all other requisites for the sustenance of the path, and offer them to the Sangha of the four quarters and to the various worthy sages."
"You all should accept the invitation;
if you do not accept it, you will incur transgression.
Judging by this, the sages and saints are not far away; when their response is invoked, they shall appear.

If one performs meritorious deeds, one should first exert all one's strength to uphold the superior precepts, and thereafter sincerely invite the Sangha of the four quarters and the various worthy sages.
If one cannot do so for a lifetime, it is well even to do so for a single day and night.
If one is unable to do so, one should accept the offerings at the time they are presented and cease once the ceremony concludes.
All these worthy sages come to receive the invitation; if there is any transgression, one must repent according to the Dharma.
All these transgressions committed by a bodhisattva constitute the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
One should perform the ritual confession according to the Dharma before those capable of explaining and receiving the repentance within either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.
"If a bodhisattva, through intense afflictions (*kleśa*), commits an offense involving a *pārājika* matter, they lose the discipline of the precepts (*saṃvara-śīla*) and should receive them again.

If they commit an offense involving a *pārājika* matter through middling afflictions, they should kneel with palms joined before three or more persons and perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Having committed many offenses, one makes this declaration:
"Venerable sir, take note!
I, [name], renounce the Bodhisattva Vinaya."
Regarding the matters mentioned, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The rest is as explained in the method for confessing *duṣkṛta* offenses of a bhikṣu.
"If one commits an offense involving a *pārājika* ground due to minor afflictions, or other offenses, one should confess them before a single person."
The Text for the Three Prostrations:

“May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm—the world-nature and the six realms of existence—whose three karmas are shrouded by the defilements and delusions of sinful obstructions, topple the mountain of inversion, exhaust the four currents, ascend the path of equality, and enter the realm of non-action.”
I take refuge and pay homage to the Buddha Vairocana of the seven locations and eight assemblies, and to all the Honored Ones of Perfect Enlightenment throughout the lands of the ten directions.

"May the sentient beings of the six realms within the world-nature of the dharma-realm of the ten directions—who have sunk into and are long submerged in the various states of existence—have the forest of precepts destroyed and false illumination extinguished."
I take refuge and pay homage to the Buddha-Flower Adornment Treasury (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*) of the seven locations and eight assemblies, the ocean of sūtras throughout the lands of the ten directions.

"I vow that within the dharma-realm of the ten directions, may all sentient beings of the six realms—the nature of the world—who are bound by narrow-mindedness and steeped in perversion, suddenly sever their biased perceptions and the conceptualizations of abiding; may they forever attach themselves to the Mahāyāna for as long as the future endures."
I take refuge and pay homage to the assembly of Samantabhadra and all the noble Sangha of sages throughout the lands of the ten directions.
"When one wishes to set out with the resolve for enlightenment, one should establish five vows:
first, may I quickly cast off this body."
Second, I vow that my teachers, the Sangha, and my parents shall be free from sorrow and vexation, and that my own life and spirit may swiftly reach Bodhi.
Third, I vow that when I go to practice in an araṇya, even if tigers, wolves, or venomous beasts come to devour me, I shall feel no fear, just as a bhikṣu experiences the bliss of the third dhyāna.

Fourth, if I go to a forest hermitage (āraṇya) and rain falls or wind rises, or if there are evil spirits or venomous dragons that come wishing to sting me, my mind remains peaceful and secure, and I feel no fear.

It is like a person wishing to cross the great ocean who, upon reaching its center, is suddenly struck by a wind that raises massive waves; the one attempting to cross becomes terrified, but when the celestial wind subsides, they reach the further shore with a heart full of great joy.
May I likewise swiftly reach the unsurpassed shore of Bodhi.
Fifth, may I dwell in an araṇya; should I fall ill, may the devas come to my side to instruct me so that my mind remains free from regret.
I further reflected:
"Within this body of mine dwell four venomous snakes together, just as four snakes might share a single den.

When the snakes wish to emerge, they each say to one another, 'I shall go first,' and thus quarreling over the den, they do not leave and die within it; because of their mutual anger and contention, all four perish together."
"I now have four venomous snakes within my body; they contend with one another and harbor anger within me.

When he reflects thus, his illness is immediately cured, the bodhicitta arises, and his mind attains peace. His six consciousnesses are no longer distracted; he settles his mind in the araṇya, fulfilling the four practices, and settles his mind in dhyāna-samādhi to subdue the six sense-faculties.
This was the fifth vow.
Having made this vow, he prostrated to the Buddhas of the four directions, performing ten bows and speaking these words:
"O World-Honored Buddhas!
Have compassion for us and protect us, enabling us to attain the Unsurpassed Way and swiftly reach Bodhi. I now repent.
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha, as well as in the ten stages of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and all other worthy sages.

Since countless kalpas past, I have wandered through birth and death—through hundreds, thousands, and immeasurable billions of lifetimes—sometimes falling into the six realms of existence to undergo diverse retributions, or becoming hungry ghosts or animals, enduring such suffering and never attaining happiness.

I have reflected upon myself and found that I am entangled by my own delusions; I do not behold the Noble Path, which obstructs the gate to Nirvana and closes the door to the Deathless. It blocks all paths of wholesome merit, prevents me from hearing the True Dharma, and causes me to sink into the great ocean—such are my bitter sufferings and transgressions.
"Now I confess all [sins] while prostrating with my five limbs upon the ground.
One should likewise prostrate seven times.
While prostrating, one should utter these words:

"May you remove the immeasurable poisons from my body; may you extract the immeasurable poisons of deviance and folly; may you extract the immeasurable dust-like delusions of deviance and folly, so that my mind and intentions become pure and the six recollections are accomplished."

May I reach the forest hermitage (āraṇya) with a mind free from fear and swiftly attain Bodhi; may I open the gate of Nirvāṇa and unlock the door of the Deathless Nectar (amṛta); may I block the gates of hell and close the paths of the three evil realms; may I uproot the three poisons and escape the net of the triple world; may I obtain the three joys and realize the three fruits; may I directly transcend the perils of birth and death, attain wisdom, leave behind my final body, and swiftly reach Bodhi.
Having made this vow, he rose from the ground; after paying homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, he stood with palms joined, his heart filled with joy, and thought to himself:
"My transgressions are forever eradicated."
"There are four methods for accepting the corded couch:
first, to invite the Buddha;
second, to invite one's teacher;"
Third, put on leather sandals and bare the right shoulder to become pure;
fourth, kneel with the right knee touching the ground before the Buddha.
Then request the preceptor to make the following formal announcement:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions and Mahākāśyapa personally received the dharma of araṇya from before the Buddha; the Buddha acts as the witness, and the teacher acts as the knower."

"If for forty-five days I have practiced asceticism with a resolve that does not waver, yet were I to give rise to a thought of retreat, I would be speaking falsely and deceiving all the devas, failing to reach the further shore."
"Venerable sir, please bear witness!
Then, request the teacher to speak as follows:
"Elder, attend with one-pointed mind!"
"I now make this vow before the Buddha, requesting the Virtuous One to bear witness.
'If you should retreat, you will deceive others and fall into hell yourself, where you shall not escape suffering.'"
"You should truly accomplish the practice of an araṇya-dweller and attain araṇya-wisdom.
Maintain this accordingly. He replied:
"So be it," he said three times.
"This is the ritual for receiving the khakkhara staff."
Kneeling before the Virtuous One, he spoke thus three times:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I now request the Virtuous One to be my teacher."
Thus he requested three times.
The Venerable One spoke as follows:
"Elder, attend closely!
Now that you have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, you should receive and uphold this according to the Dharma.
You must not enter the monastic quarters with impure hands; you should remove your sandals and must not stand near the ground.
If one enters the house of a layperson, one should follow behind.

If one must visit the house of a layperson before midday, or if one is to receive a midday meal for various reasons, one should call out three times; if they do not come after the third call, one should call up to five times; if they still do not come after the fifth call, one should call up to seven times.
"Seventh, if she does not come back, go to other houses;
even if you go to seven houses and do not receive it from those seven houses," then the second and third [attempts] are also explained in this same manner.
The Precept for Renouncing the Dharma:
"Venerable one, attend to me with a single mind!

This bhikṣu [name], who observes the five precepts and the deportment of an upāsaka, for what reason shall he live out his full lifespan without dying prematurely, and not fall into the intermediate state of hell?"
"I inform the Buddhas of the ten directions and Mahākāśyapa: all of you should listen well.
So-and-so has thus erected the marker.
Having made this announcement three times, once he has finished grasping the marker and completed its erection, he again makes the following announcement:
“May all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the virtuous ones of pure conduct in the four quarters bear witness:
I do not deceive the devas; I have not yet reached the other shore.”
Now I bring this Dharma-seat and the appropriate staff, both of which are complete.
I now enter the retreat; all bhikṣus who practice in the araṇya shall likewise enter the retreat.
Having thus addressed him three times and performed six prostrations, he joined his palms with a single mind and thought thus:
"I call upon the Buddhas of the ten directions and Mahākāśyapa!"
"Venerable [Name] bhikṣu, [Name] upāsaka, the assembly’s mindfulness is established.
Now that we have released our seats and moved elsewhere, we shall resume the formal connection.
When one wishes to take hold of a rope bed, one should practice the four foundations of mindfulness.
The first thought is to reflect that everything within my body is impermanent and should be regarded as suffering.
Second, by practicing the cultivation of the body as suffering, the wisdom of emptiness will naturally arise; one should accordingly cultivate this.
Third, one should give rise to a mind of forbearance and not harbor anger.
Fourth, one should give rise to a mind of joy; if one gives rise to a mind of joy, one will swiftly reach Bodhi.
Having formed these thoughts, one will be completely freed from those cattle-herders, tigers, and wolves, as well as loud and soft noises, lewd sounds, and oppressions.
Having distanced oneself from these sounds, one should settle the mind and maintain upright mindfulness.
When wishing to eliminate all defilements, one should form two thoughts, saying:
"First, may my body attain tranquil concentration, so that without giving rise to exhaustion, I may swiftly reach Bodhi."

"Second, you shall attain a mind of leisure and tranquility, free from confusion, and with the six consciousnesses at peace, you shall attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Having spoken thus, he calmly descended from his seat, stood before the Buddha, and prostrated himself ten times.
Standing with palms joined, he immediately formed three recollections:
first, the recollection of the Buddha; second, the recollection of the precepts; and third, the recollection of meditative concentration.
Having performed these recollections, he sat down calmly upon his rope-couch.
Furthermore, one should practice the six recollections:
first, the recollection that all Buddhas protect me and that my own recollection is perfected;
second, the recollection that my aggregate of precepts is pure—where "precepts" refers to the *prātimokṣa* and "recollection" means not transgressing them.

From the introductory section to the verses, one should contemplate four matters until reaching thirteen; by recollecting these thirteen, one accomplishes the two indeterminate rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the ninety *pāyattika* rules, the four *pratideśanīya* rules, the numerous rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). From the top down, all should be recollected with truthfulness.
Third, one should reflect upon repaying the kindness of one's parents, teachers, and the Sangha.
Fourth, one should reflect that the five desires are all impermanent, the root of great affliction, and the primary cause of the net of delusion.
Fifth, one should contemplate the suffering and affliction of the hells, and diligently cultivate goodness to remain far removed from such suffering.
Having already left the household life, I ought to be prudent, abandoning evil and practicing goodness.

Sixth is mindfulness of wisdom: if I possess wisdom, I should maintain it through recollection; when wisdom is perfected, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished, and one attains the Unsurpassed Way.
With these six recollections fully perfected, one sits with a settled mind.
According to the method of meditation:
"If a lay follower wishes to move about, he should maintain three reflections:

first, he should reflect that as he walks, there are many insects and ants crawling upon the ground; if he should inadvertently kill them, what offense would he incur? [He should reflect that] those who die [from his carelessness] will be reborn in heaven."
Second, one should mindfully practice in accordance with the Dharma; holding the staff upright in one's hand like an upturned palm, one should proceed with dignified deportment, composed and serene.
Third, while walking, one should not look back, nor should one shake the head or move the hands.
This is called the accomplishment of the three mindfulnesses.
When an upāsaka who practices according to the Dharma approaches with a reverent demeanor and sincere faith, bringing food, one should receive it with purity.
Having finished receiving [the food], he sat down in the full lotus posture and further practiced four recollections:
first, he recollected that within his body there were eighty thousand families of worms, and that these worms would all find peace and security upon obtaining this food.

Second, one should reflect: "When I receive food, I shall eat but little; if I eat little, my body will become light; if the body is light, my various desires will also diminish; and if desires are diminished, I will swiftly attain Bodhi."
Third, I do not eat for the sake of beauty, but solely for the sustenance of life;
when all wholesome qualities are accomplished, one achieves unsurpassed wisdom.
Fourth, at the time of my eating, I shall cause all hungry beings throughout the ten directions to be fully satisfied; this is how they should all practice.
